did_you_know.text: Did you know? On the thirteenth day of Adar, the day appointed for the Jews to be attacked, the situation was reversed: the Jews gained control over those who hated them and fought those seeking their harm.
Did you know? The officials and royal administrators supported the Jews because they feared Mordecai, whose position in the royal palace continued to rise.
Did you know? Although the Jews were permitted to attack their enemies, the text emphasizes that they did not take any plunder—not in Susa nor in the king’s provinces.
Did you know? On the first day, five hundred men and Haman’s ten sons were killed in Susa; afterward, Esther requested an additional day of fighting in Susa.
Did you know? In the rest of the king’s provinces, seventy-five thousand enemies of the Jews were killed, and there too the text states that the Jews took no plunder.

Did you know? The day of rest depended on the location: the Jews in the provinces rested on the fourteenth day of Adar, while the Jews in Susa, who also fought on the fourteenth, rested on the fifteenth.
Did you know? The Purim customs established in this chapter include feasting and rejoicing, sending gifts to one another, and giving gifts to the poor.
Did you know? The name “Purim” is explicitly connected to the “pur,” the lot cast by Haman to determine the date for the destruction of the Jews.

Did you know? Mordecai decreed that the days of Purim should be remembered and celebrated in every generation, in every family, province, and city, and that their memory should never disappear from among the Jews.
Did you know? Esther and Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews throughout the king’s provinces to strengthen the observance of Purim at its appointed times, and these matters were recorded in a book.
